The filings as a panel: one row per company and year

Source: R/xbrl_panel.R
xbrl_panel.Rd

Everything before this is about reading filings correctly; this is where they become data to analyse. One row per filing and basis, the statement figures as named variables – revenue, operating_profit, equity, cash, cf_operating – beside who the company is and how far its figures can be trusted. A time series of one company and a cross-section of many are the same table, so whatever is computed from it works on either.

Usage

xbrl_panel(x, basis = "parent", standardise = TRUE, .checks = NULL)

Arguments

x

A tibble from read_xbrl(), or from xbrl_validate(), whose lines and checks are then read rather than computed again.

basis

"parent" (default), "consolidated", or both. A filing with group accounts has a row for each basis asked for.

standardise

Run xbrl_standardise() first, if it has not been. Default TRUE.

.checks

Internal: the checks xbrl_screen() has already run on the same facts, as attr(s, "checks"), so they are not run twice.

Value

A tibble of class cvrr_panel: the key (cvr, name, period_start, period_end), basis, the figures, the background (class, form, micro, founded, assurance, opinion_kind, going_concern, in_group, group_accounts, employees, currency), the trust columns, and file. Amounts are in the reporting currency as filed.

Where the figures come from

From xbrl_lines(), not from the facts directly: a line the filer left out of the balance sheet is derived there, a line tagged twice is settled, and after xbrl_standardise() a figure in the wrong unit is already in the right one. Each variable is read from a list of elements, the first one the filing reports winning; the lists are in attr(p, "variables").

Most Danish filings are accounting class B, which may start the income statement at the gross profit. revenue is then NA, not an estimate: 13% of a 4,304-filing corpus report it, against 81% the gross profit.

Signs

One convention throughout. Incomes, balances and subtotals keep their natural sign, so a loss is negative and so is negative equity. Costs are positive amounts: 99% of filers write them so, and the rest have signed them already. Tax is the one cost that is genuinely negative – a refund, a deferred tax asset – in a fifth of filings, so where the result before and after tax are both reported it is their difference, which has the right sign by construction, and net_financials is likewise the result before tax less the operating result.

That makes net_financials the complete figure and finance_income and finance_expenses only the lines called that. Income from subsidiaries and impairment of financial assets are financial items too, and with them left out the two lines account for the result before tax in 77% of the corpus. Use net_financials for the total.

How far to trust a row

balance_reconciled, income_reconciled and cashflow_reconciled are the verdicts of check_statement(), check_cascade() and check_cashflow(); corrections counts the figures xbrl_standardise() changed in the filing. A row is kept whatever they say: excluding is the analysis's decision, and it can only be made if the row is there.

See also

xbrl_lines() for the statements line by line, xbrl_screen() for what does not add up.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
x <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl")
p <- xbrl_panel(x)

# one company over time
p[p$cvr == "12345678", c("period_end", "gross_profit", "operating_profit", "equity")]

# the rows whose statements add up
subset(p, balance_reconciled & income_reconciled)
} # }
